chunks.text: The standardized shipping container, popularized by Malcom McLean in 1956, is a steel box of fixed dimensions that can be moved seamlessly between ships, trucks, and trains. It dramatically lowered the cost and time of moving goods, helping shrink the world and enable modern global trade.

Globalization is the accelerating integration of the world's economies, societies, and cultures through the increasingly rapid movement of goods, people, money, information, and ideas across national borders. It is an acceleration of earlier networks like the Silk Roads and Columbian Exchange, not something wholly new.

Twentieth-century transportation advances — faster and larger ships, the shipping container, the jet airliner, and improved roads, trucks, and railroads — slashed the cost and time of moving goods and people, making physical distance matter less for trade and travel.

The jet airliner, especially after the 1950s, made it possible to travel between continents in hours rather than weeks, moving people, mail, and high-value goods at unprecedented speed and binding distant places more tightly together.
Communication technologies — the telephone, radio, television, and satellites — progressively shrank the world by enabling rapid, then near-instant, contact and broadcasting across great distances.

Computers grew exponentially more powerful and cheaper, transforming how information is processed, and from the late twentieth century the internet, the World Wide Web, and mobile phones connected billions of people into a single instantaneous network for information, money, and ideas.

Modern technologies enabled dense global exchange: complex supply chains in which a product is designed in one country, built from parts made in several others, and sold everywhere, along with enormous cross-border financial flows and the rapid spread of media and ideas.

Technology was the enabler of modern globalization: it created the infrastructure on which globalization was built by radically lowering the cost and time of moving goods, people, money, and information, even though it did not by itself cause every economic and cultural change.

The Green Revolution was a set of mid-twentieth-century agricultural innovations — high-yield varieties of wheat and rice combined with chemical fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation, and mechanization — that dramatically increased food production, especially in the developing world.

Spread to countries like India, Mexico, and the Philippines from the 1940s through the 1970s, the Green Revolution allowed food production to keep pace with soaring population growth, helping avert the mass famines many experts had predicted and saving perhaps a billion people from starvation.

The Green Revolution also had real costs: it required expensive inputs like fertilizers, machinery, and fuel that favored wealthier farmers and deepened rural inequality, relied on chemicals and irrigation that damaged soils and depleted water, and reduced crop diversity.

The same connections that move goods and ideas also move pathogens. In a densely connected world, a disease emerging in one place can reach the entire planet with frightening speed, continuing a pattern seen with plague on the Silk Roads and disease in the Columbian Exchange.

The influenza pandemic of 1918–1919 (the 'Spanish flu'), spread in part by the movement of soldiers at the end of World War I, infected perhaps a third of humanity and killed an estimated 50 million people or more — more than the war itself.

The COVID-19 pandemic that began in 2019 spread across the globe within weeks via air travel, demonstrating how interconnected and how vulnerable the modern world is, and how much faster disease now travels than in 1918.

As people grew wealthier and lived longer and medicine conquered many infectious diseases, the leading causes of death increasingly shifted toward chronic, non-communicable conditions like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, associated with longer life and modern diets and lifestyles.

The interconnected world produced powerful new tools to fight disease: vaccines, antibiotics, and global health campaigns of unprecedented reach, delivered through international cooperation and organizations like the World Health Organization.

The global eradication of smallpox, declared in 1980 after a worldwide vaccination campaign coordinated by the World Health Organization, was the most dramatic medical triumph of the era, eliminating a disease that had killed hundreds of millions over the centuries.

Comparing the 1918 flu and COVID-19 shows continuity and change: both were fast-spreading global respiratory pandemics, but COVID-19 spread far faster via air travel (deeper globalization) and met a far more powerful response (rapid virus identification, genome sequencing, instant data-sharing, and vaccines within a year).

Both the 1918 and COVID-19 pandemics exposed inequalities (the poor and marginalized suffered most), provoked debates over individual liberty versus public health, and showed that even advanced societies remain vulnerable to nature.

Analyzing a development's benefits and costs requires stating it clearly, identifying concrete benefits and concrete costs with evidence, and then weighing them — including who benefited and who bore the costs — rather than presenting it as purely good or purely bad.

Globalization is double-edged: the same forces that brought cheap goods, instant communication, food for billions, and powerful medicine also brought environmental damage, the rapid global spread of disease and financial crises, cultural disruption, and benefits distributed very unequally.

Disease in the globalized era continues an old pattern at a new scale: the Black Death on the Silk Roads, smallpox in the Columbian Exchange, the 1918 influenza, and COVID-19 form a continuity-and-change thread in which interconnection spreads disease ever faster while medical responses grow stronger.
